transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doc, to be completely honest with you, I didn't even want to come in today, but my hands are kind of tied here. I've been doing freight and material moving for a long time—you know, warehouse stuff, loading, unloading, being on your feet for ten, twelve hours a shift. I took some college classes back in the day, but physical labor is the work I know and the work I'm good at. 

Anyway, I was up for this new logistics job, a really good contract with solid hours, and they send you to their own corporate clinic for a physical clearance. Standard stuff, right? They check your blood pressure, your vision, your lifting capacity, all that. But the doctor there—he takes one look at the scale and tells me he can't clear me. He actually refused to sign the paperwork because he said my weight was too low. Too low! Can you believe that? 

I tried explaining to him that when you're moving heavy stock all day, you don't want a bunch of extra bulk weighing you down. You're constantly pivoting, lifting, carrying... it's demanding. To me, I look in the mirror and I just see a guy who's lean. I'm stripped down to the essentials. I just look like someone who is ready to work and stay quick on his feet, you know? You can't be dragging yourself around when you've got a quota to meet. But he wouldn't listen, and they said I had to come see someone like you before they'd even reconsider putting me on the schedule. So, here I am, just trying to jump through their hoops so I can get back on the floor.
Do you think your weight is currently too low?

Too low? No, look... I mean, I really don't. It is funny you ask it exactly like that, though, because that is exactly what my sister keeps harping on. Her and that corporate doctor, they are just a broken record. They keep saying I am in some kind of immediate danger. My sister called me just the other night, practically in tears, going on and on about how she is worried sick, how my weight is dangerously low and she thinks I am going to collapse or something. And then this doctor at the clearance clinic pulls the exact same routine, acting like I am about to drop dead right there on his linoleum floor. 

But they are just making it so much bigger than it actually is. They are blowing the whole thing way out of proportion because, honestly, neither of them has a clue what my day-to-day life actually requires. My sister sits at a computer all day, and that doctor, well, he just sits in an exam room checking boxes. They do not understand the mechanics of moving freight for a living. I have tried to explain it to them, I really have. I tell them, look, I am just keeping myself light. I am keeping myself sharp. When you are out there on the warehouse floor, dodging forklifts, swinging heavy boxes onto pallets for twelve hours, you need to be agile. If you have extra weight on your frame, it just slows your reaction time down, it wears out your knees and your back faster... it is just basic physics, right? 

I am just keeping myself ready for work. That is literally all this is. I am perfectly conditioned for the job. But they just look at some standard medical chart on a wall and decide I am in danger, completely ignoring the fact that I am out-working guys half my age every single shift. So no, doc, I do not think it is too low at all. I think it is exactly where it needs to be for me to do what I do best, and I just wish people would stop overreacting and let me get back to it.
Do you think you look underweight when you look in the mirror?

Well, no, not underweight. I mean, when I look in the mirror... it's complicated, I guess. Because I look at myself, especially right around the middle, you know, my stomach and my waist, and I don't see someone who's wasting away. I see someone who needs to stay tight. 

It's like this... when you're on the floor for a twelve-hour shift, your core is everything. Every time you twist to grab a crate, every time you brace yourself to lift a pallet jack, it all comes from the center. And over the years, I've just developed this mindset, this standard for myself. If I look in that mirror and I'm not completely tight, if there's any softness or if I'm not absolutely smaller and streamlined right there around the waist... I just feel like I'm losing my edge. I feel like I'm not that same disciplined guy who can out-lift the twenty-somethings. 

It's about discipline, doc. It really is. I've always prided myself on being the hardest worker in the room, the guy who never calls out, the guy who can keep going when everyone else is taking a breather. And that discipline, it has to show physically. If I let myself get soft, if I don't look completely lean and tight in the mirror, it feels like a personal failure. It feels like I'm letting myself go, like I'm losing the one thing I've always been able to control, which is my work ethic and my physical readiness. So no, I don't see "underweight." I see a guy who is trying desperately to maintain his discipline, to stay tight and ready for the demands of the job, because if I'm not that guy, then who am I out there on the warehouse floor?
Are you afraid of gaining weight?

Well, "afraid" is a strong word, doc, but... yeah, I guess you could say that. I mean, it's more about control and just knowing my body. Like, if I even think about eating something heavy—say, a bowl of rice, or some thick bread, or anything that's got too much grease or oil in it—my mind just starts racing. I can't stop thinking about it. I just picture that heavy food sitting right there in my gut, turning straight into fat, just weighing me down almost instantly. 

It's like this constant loop in my head. I'll eat something like that, maybe if I'm at a family thing and my sister pushes a plate in front of me, and for the rest of the night, I'm just hyper-aware of how my stomach feels. I can almost feel it expanding, you know? And then, I can't even sleep right because I'm just waiting for morning. The second I wake up, before I even have a glass of water, I have to step on the scale. I just have to know. Or I'll grab my work belt—the heavy leather one I wear on the floor—and I'll pull it tight just to check the notch. I have to make sure it still hits that exact same hole it always does. 

If it feels even a fraction of an inch tighter, or if the scale bumps up even a tiny bit, it just ruins my whole day. I feel like I've completely let myself go, like I've lost that discipline I was just talking about. Because in my line of work, you start putting on weight, you start getting sluggish, and before you know it, you're the guy they're rotating out for the younger crew. I can't let that happen. So yeah, I guess I am terrified of putting on weight, because to me, gaining weight means losing my edge, losing my job, losing everything I've built my life around. I just can't risk it for a piece of bread, you know? It's just not worth the anxiety it puts me through.
When you look in the mirror, do you see your actual weight or do you see something different?

Well, see, the thing is... I don't really know what "actual weight" is even supposed to look like, to be perfectly honest with you. I don't look in the bathroom mirror in the morning and see a number. Like I was trying to explain just a minute ago, it's really about what that reflection represents. When I stand there, you know, usually right after I wake up, the lighting in my bathroom catches every angle, and I zero right in on my stomach and my waist. That's the real proving ground. 

If I stand there and I don't see that I'm smaller, if I don't see that my core is completely tight-looking right across the middle... well, I don't see a guy who's "too thin," I see a guy who is slipping. I feel like if I'm not smaller and tight-looking, then I'm just not the disciplined man I used to be on the warehouse floor. And that's a hard pill to swallow, doc. Because you have to understand my history there. I started moving freight when I was twenty-two years old. Back then, I could throw eighty-pound sacks of concrete over my shoulder all day and still have the energy to go out after. Now I'm fifty-five. The only thing separating me from the guys who got washed out, the guys who blew out their backs or just couldn't keep up the pace and got let go, is my absolute discipline. 

So when I look in that mirror, I'm looking for proof that I still have it. If my waist looks even a little bit soft, or if I don't look as small and compact as I need to be to maneuver around those pallets, my mind just goes straight to, "You're losing it. You're getting sloppy." It's not about seeing some distorted fun-house mirror thing, it's about seeing the truth of my work ethic. If I don't look small and tight, I just feel like a fraud. I feel like I'm turning into one of those guys who has to ask the younger crew for help lifting a crate, and I will absolutely not be that guy. I refuse. So I guess I don't see "weight," doc. I see my discipline, and I have to make sure it's still there every single day.
Do you restrict what you eat because you're afraid of gaining weight?

Well, restrict... I mean, I guess that’s one word for it, doc. It just goes right back to what I was saying about the discipline and not getting sluggish. Listen, when you're working a twelve-hour shift moving pallets, you don't have time to be bogged down by a heavy stomach anyway. You just don't. I see these young guys, these kids really, they come into the breakroom with these massive fast-food bags, eating burgers and fries, and then they're dragging their feet for the next four hours. They're sweating, they're slow, they're complaining about their backs. I can't do that. I absolutely refuse to be that guy. 

So, yeah, I keep things very, very controlled. Most days, honestly, I just keep it to black coffee. I'll bring a big thermos of it and that just keeps the engine running, you know? It gives me the energy without the weight. Maybe, if I really feel like I need something solid to get through the last few hours, I'll have a boiled egg, or maybe just a little bit of tuna out of a can. It's clean, it's light, and most importantly, it doesn't sit in my gut and make me feel like I'm expanding and getting soft. 

And the thing is, if I have a day off—which isn't often, because I pick up the overtime whenever they offer it, I like to stay busy—but if I'm at home and I'm not actually out there moving freight on a shift, well... my mind just starts rationalizing it. I tell myself I don’t need a real meal anyway. It just doesn't make sense to put fuel in the tank if the truck isn't moving, right? Because if I sit down and eat a full meal on a day off, that's when that anxiety really kicks into overdrive. That's when I feel like I'm just sitting in my recliner letting the food turn straight into fat, just completely ruining all that hard work and discipline I've built up all week. So I just don't do it. I stick to the coffee, I stick to the bare minimum, because the alternative—feeling that softness, feeling like I'm losing control—is just something I can't live with.
Does your fear of gaining weight affect what you eat or do on days when you're not working?

Well, yeah, like I... like I was just saying a minute ago, doc, it absolutely does. Honestly, the days off are almost harder than the days I'm on the floor. Because when I'm at the warehouse, I have a rhythm, you know? I have the pallets, the schedule, the sweat, the constant motion. But on a Sunday, if I don't pick up an overtime shift—which, like I said, I try to do just to avoid this exact situation—but if I'm stuck at home, that fear just kind of takes over everything. 

I mean, I know I just told you that most days I keep it to black coffee, maybe a boiled egg or a little tuna. But when I'm at home and I'm not moving freight on a shift, I just completely lock it down. I tell myself I don't need a real meal anyway. And I really believe that. I mean, why would I? It's just basic mechanics to me. If your truck is parked in the driveway, you don't keep pumping gas into it, right? It'll just overflow. And that's exactly how I picture my body. 

If I'm just sitting in my living room, maybe trying to watch a game or read the paper, and I even think about eating something substantial, I can literally feel the panic rising up in my chest. I start thinking about how I'm not burning it off. I think about how every single bite is just going to settle right around my waistline and make me soft. So I just stick to the coffee. I'll brew a whole pot in the morning and just nurse it all day long. Sometimes I'll catch myself pacing around the house, doing yard work I don't even need to do, fixing hinges that aren't even squeaking, just to keep moving. Because if I sit still, my mind starts telling me I'm getting lazy, that I'm losing my edge, that I'm putting on weight just by sitting in the recliner. 

So, yeah, my days off are completely dictated by it. I just don't eat a real meal on those days, period. It's just not worth the mental gymnastics I have to go through if I do. It's so much easier to just feel empty than to sit there feeling... heavy. You know what I mean? It's just about keeping the discipline tight, even when nobody is watching. Especially when nobody is watching.
Has your fear of gaining weight ever caused you to avoid social gatherings or events where food is involved?

Well, yeah, I avoid them like the plague now. I really do. Because you go to these things—like, the guys from the loading dock, they like to do these Friday night get-togethers, maybe head down to the pub near the rail yard, or somebody hosts a barbecue at their place. And it’s always just a mountain of the worst possible stuff. It’s all heavy carbs and fried junk. 

And the thing is, doc, I just can't handle being around that kind of food anymore, let alone eating it. If I go, they're going to push it on me. "Hey, grab a plate, have a bun, eat some of this." But if I cave... if I eat rice, or bread, or something greasy like those wings or burgers they always order, it just completely derails my mind. I can’t stop thinking it will sit on me right away. I mean that literally. I'll be sitting there in a folding chair, trying to make small talk about the forklift maintenance schedule or whatever, but my brain is just screaming at me. I can actually feel the grease and the bread just... expanding in my gut, turning into dead weight, just sitting there attaching itself to my waistline while I'm still at the party. 

It completely ruins the night, and then it ruins the next day, too. Because I'll go home, I'll toss and turn, and the next morning, the very first thing I have to do—before I even think about brewing that pot of coffee I told you about—is I have to check. I'll step right on the scale, and then I'll pull on my work pants and pull my belt tight, right to the notch I always use. I'll check the scale or my belt the next morning to make absolutely sure I didn’t let myself go. If that belt feels even a fraction of a millimeter tighter, or if the number on that scale blinks even a point higher, I feel like a total failure. I feel like I've just thrown away years of discipline for a stupid piece of bread. 

So, it's just not worth it. I tell the guys I'm busy. I tell them I've got chores, or I'm trying to catch some sleep before an early shift. I make up whatever excuse I need to. Because the mental torture of eating that greasy stuff and then waking up in a panic, yanking at my belt loops to prove to myself I'm not getting soft... it's just too much, doc. It's so much easier to just stay home and keep the engine running clean.
Have you avoided any important life events or activities because of your concerns about weight?

Well, avoided? I mean... besides the social stuff with the guys that I just told you about, it's actually kind of the other way around right now, doc. It’s not so much me avoiding things, it’s... well, it’s life kind of blocking me out, and I'll tell you, it is incredibly frustrating. 

See, I’ve been trying to make a move lately. I applied for this new logistics job—a really good setup, better pay, moving up a bit from just strictly hauling pallets on the floor to actually coordinating the freight lines and managing the dock schedule. I’ve got the experience, I’ve got a bit of college under my belt from years ago, and I know the warehouse floor better than anyone they could possibly bring in off the street. I nailed the interviews, right? They loved me. 

But then, you know how corporate works, you have to do the standard physical. The medical clearance. And... well, they flagged me. The clinic they sent me to, the doctor there took one look at my chart, looked at my weight, started asking me a bunch of questions about my eating habits—honestly, probably the exact same kind of stuff you're asking me right now—and suddenly, the brakes are completely pumped. 

The new logistics job won’t clear me to start until I get this addressed. They literally put my start date on ice. So my eating and my weight... it's put my entire work plans on hold. And the craziest part about all of this is that I keep telling myself—and I told the HR lady, too—I’m job-ready! I am completely ready to go right this second. I told them, look, I have more energy and discipline than guys half my age. I run a tight ship, I keep the engine clean, I don't get sluggish after lunch because I don't bog myself down with heavy food. I'm the hardest worker they're ever going to hire. 

But they just look at the numbers. Because of their liability rules or insurance or whatever it is, they won't let me on the dock until somebody signs a piece of paper saying my weight is quote-unquote "acceptable." So now I'm just stuck. I'm sitting around, not working the new job, worrying about my weight, pacing around my house doing nothing. It’s just... it’s maddening, doc. Work is what keeps me grounded, it's what keeps me moving, and now this whole thing is the exact reason I can't even clock in.
Are there any personal relationships in your life that have been affected by your concerns about your weight?

Well, my sister... yeah, it’s really put a wedge between me and my sister lately. She just won't let it go. She lives a couple of towns over, and it used to be we’d just talk on Sundays, you know, catch up on her kids, how the house is holding up, normal family stuff. But now? Now every single time the phone rings and it's her, I know exactly what the conversation is going to turn into. It's a whole interrogation. 

She and that clinic doctor—the one holding up my job—they’re basically a broken record at this point. My sister and the doctor keep saying I’m in danger. Danger! Can you believe that? They act like I’m just going to drop dead at any second. My sister will literally cry on the phone, telling me my heart's going to give out, and they're both just making it so much bigger than it actually is. It is completely blown out of proportion. 

It’s incredibly frustrating because they just don’t understand. Neither of them gets what it takes to do what I do, or how my body actually works. They sit at desks all day, but I’m on my feet, I’m moving freight, I'm managing a chaotic floor. I’ve tried to explain it to her, I really have. I told her last week, "Look, I am just keeping myself light. I'm keeping myself sharp." If I eat the way she wants me to eat, I’ll get sluggish, I'll get soft, and I’ll lose my edge. I am just staying lean and ready for work, you know? Like a finely tuned machine. 

But she doesn't listen. She just keeps bringing up the fact that I look too thin or whatever the doctor put on that stupid medical clearance form. It's gotten to the point where I don't even want to pick up the phone when she calls, because I just don't have the energy to defend myself again. I just want to be left alone to manage my own engine so I can get back on the dock where I belong, but they just keep treating me like I'm some sort of tragedy waiting to happen.
Have you ever felt like your concerns about weight have affected your ability to enjoy daily activities or maintain relationships with family and friends?

Well, I mean... we just talked about my sister and the guys from the loading dock, so you know how that is going right now. But as far as me personally not enjoying my daily activities? I don't really see it that way at all, doc. I mean, what even is enjoyment, right? 

For my sister, enjoyment is sitting around eating a heavy Sunday pot roast and watching television until she falls asleep on the couch. For the guys at work, it's drinking cheap beer and eating fried junk until they are completely bloated and useless the next morning. I don't want any part of that. I actually enjoy my routine. I enjoy the discipline of it. I like waking up at four thirty in the morning, knowing I am light, knowing I am sharp. I get up, I make my black coffee—just one cup, brewed really strong, usually a dark roast—and I know my body is running exactly the way I need it to. I will go out for a walk before the sun is even up, and that is my enjoyment right there. Just me, the crisp morning air, no heavy food dragging me down, no grease sitting in my gut. I feel energized. I feel like I could outwork any twenty-something they try to put on that warehouse floor with me. 

So when you ask if my concerns are ruining my relationships or my life... I mean, I guess it affects how other people act around me, like my sister getting all hysterical on the phone. But I am not the one who changed. I am just trying to live my life and keep myself in top shape for the freight lines. It is them who can not seem to handle it. They are the ones making it a huge deal. If everyone would just back off and let me manage my own engine, everything would be perfectly fine. I would still talk to my sister every single Sunday if she would just stick to talking about her kids instead of interrogating me about my waistline. So, no, I do not feel like my concerns are ruining my enjoyment of anything. It is everyone else making a big deal out of nothing that ruins it.
Do you feel like your concerns about weight are affecting your overall quality of life?

Quality of life... you know, it’s funny you phrase it exactly like that, doc, because I was just thinking about this the other day while I was out on my morning walk. What really makes a good quality of life? To me, it's independence. It's capability. It's knowing that your engine is running clean and you don't have to rely on anybody else to get the job done. 

I look at guys my age—I'm fifty-five—and I look at the guys I've worked with on the freight lines for years. You want to talk about quality of life? They’re waking up groaning, their knees are shot, their lower backs are completely blown out, and they’re taking a handful of pills every morning for their blood pressure or their cholesterol just to make it through a shift. And why? Because they spent the last thirty years eating garbage and letting themselves get soft. They get winded just climbing into the cab of a forklift. 

My quality of life, physically, is better than it has ever been. I don't have those problems. I wake up and I feel light. I feel completely dialed in. I keep my house spotless, I keep my routine tight, and I know exactly what I’m capable of. I can route a truck, I can manage a dock schedule, and I can out-hustle any of the new kids they bring in. That is a fantastic quality of life, if you ask me. Having that kind of discipline? It feels good. It feels right.

So, no, my concerns about my weight aren't hurting my life at all. The only thing—the absolute *only* thing—ruining my quality of life right now is other people getting in my way. It’s that clinic doctor refusing to sign a simple medical clearance form. It’s the HR department keeping my start date on ice over some liability technicality. It’s my sister calling me up and crying on the phone instead of just having a normal conversation. 

If it weren't for all these people panicking over a number on a scale and projecting their own ideas of health onto me, my life would be a hundred percent perfect right now. I’d be clocking in, managing the new logistics job, making better money, and coming home feeling productive. So I don't see this as a "me" problem. I really don't. If everybody would just mind their own business and let me work, my quality of life would be exactly where I want it to be.
Do you feel like your weight concerns are impacting your ability to form or maintain intimate relationships?

Intimate relationships? You mean like dating? Well, I mean, I haven't really... I haven't even thought about that in a long time. It's not something that's really on my radar right now, to be perfectly honest with you, doc. 

My last serious relationship, that was years ago, back when I was still working the swing shift down at the old distribution center. We were together for a good four years, maybe five. She was a dispatcher, actually, so she understood the hours, which was nice. But eventually, it just... fizzled out. People drift apart, you know? It happens. And since then, I just haven't had the time or the inclination to get back out there. 

Dating takes so much energy, and it's so unpredictable. You have to go out to dinners, or grab drinks, or sit in crowded places where you don't know what's in the food or how it's prepared. It completely throws off your routine. And like I said before, my routine is everything to me. It's how I stay sharp. If I start going out on dates, staying up late, eating heavy meals at restaurants just to make someone else comfortable... well, that's just going to clog up the engine, isn't it? 

Plus, at fifty-five, what are you even looking for? Most women my age, they want to settle down, take cruises, go out to eat all the time, relax. I don't want to relax. I want to work. I want to keep moving. I want to stay light and capable. If I brought someone into my life right now, they wouldn't understand my schedule. They wouldn't understand why I wake up at four thirty in the morning to walk, or why I only drink my coffee black, or why I need to stay lean for the freight lines. It would just be exactly like my sister all over again—somebody constantly nagging me, telling me I need to eat more, telling me I'm too thin, telling me I need to slow down. 

I don't have the patience to explain myself to another person right now. I just want to get this medical clearance sorted out so I can get back on the dock. That's my main focus. The logistics job, the new warehouse, getting my start date unfrozen—that's what matters. Intimate relationships? They're just a distraction I really don't need or want right now. So, no, I wouldn't say my concerns are impacting my ability to form relationships, because I'm not even trying to form them in the first place. I'm perfectly fine on my own.
Do you think your weight is the same as what other people see when they look at you?

Well, I mean... I guess there's a difference, sure. But I don't think it's because I'm seeing things wrong. I think it's because they just don't get what I'm doing. 

Like my sister, right? We talked about her. She looks at me and she just sees... I don't know, she sees something to panic about. She tells me I look like a skeleton, that I'm wasting away, that I'm in some kind of immediate danger. And that clinic doctor, the one who refused to sign my clearance form so I could start the new logistics job—he's the exact same way. He took one look at the scale, looked at me, and started talking about how my BMI was dangerously low and how I was putting my heart at risk. He actually used the word "severe." He said I was in a state of severe malnutrition. 

But I look in the mirror, doc, and I just see a guy who is ready to work. I see a guy who doesn't have a gut hanging over his belt like the rest of the guys at the warehouse. I see someone who is lean, who is sharp, who has stripped away all the excess baggage so the engine can run clean. 

They keep saying I'm in danger, but they're just making it so much bigger than it actually is. They're projecting their own ideas of what a fifty-five-year-old man should look like onto me. They think because I don't look soft and bloated like every other guy my age, there must be a medical emergency. But I'm just keeping myself light. I have to be light to move fast on the floor. I have to be sharp to route the trucks and manage the dock schedule. If I carried around an extra twenty or thirty pounds like they want me to, I'd be sluggish. I'd be slow. I'd be just like those guys complaining about their knees every morning. 

So, yeah, what they see and what I see are different. But it's not because I'm blind to my own weight. I know I'm thin. I work very hard to be thin. It's just that they don't understand the purpose of it. They don't understand that this is exactly where I need to be to do my job and live my life the way I want to. They're just blowing the whole thing completely out of proportion.
Do you think your fear of gaining weight affects how you perceive your own weight?

Fear of gaining weight... well, I don't know if I'd use the word "fear," doc. It's more about being strictly vigilant. But, I mean, I guess it does get in my head a bit. Like, if I ever eat something heavy—say, a bowl of rice, or a thick slice of bread, or, God forbid, something greasy like the fried junk the other guys at the warehouse are always shoving down their throats on their fifteen-minute breaks—I just... I can’t stop thinking about it. It completely takes over my thoughts. 

It’s like I can physically feel it just sitting on me right away, you know? Like pouring thick, dirty sludge straight into a clean engine. I'll just be going about my day, but in the back of my mind, I'm feeling it weigh me down, thinking about how it's going to make me soft and sluggish on the floor. It doesn't just pass through you, stuff like that just clings to you. 

And you better believe that the very next morning, the absolute first thing I do when I roll out of bed at four thirty—before I even start my black coffee, before I do anything else—is check. I have to step right on the scale, or I'll take my heavy leather work belt and pull it tight around my waist, right to the exact same notch I always use, just to make absolutely sure I didn’t let myself go overnight. I have to know that the grease or the carbs didn't stick to me. 

So, if that's what you mean by affecting how I perceive my weight, then sure, I guess it does. Because to me, even the slightest change from eating something heavy isn't just some normal, everyday fluctuation like the clinic doctor thinks it is. It's a warning sign that I'm slipping, that I'm losing my discipline. If I don't check the belt, or if I don't check the scale, how am I supposed to know I'm still sharp? I have to check. It's the only way to prove to myself that I'm still running clean and that I haven't turned into one of those guys who gets winded walking up a flight of stairs.
Do you feel like your concerns about weight are interfering with your overall well-being or daily life in any significant way?

Interfering? Well... look, physically, like I've been saying, I feel fine. Better than fine, I'm running like a top. But... yeah, I guess you could say it's interfering in one major, incredibly frustrating way. And it's the whole reason I'm even sitting here talking to you right now, to be perfectly honest. 

It’s this new logistics job. I’ve been telling you about it. It’s a great gig at the new warehouse, managing the floor, handling the freight routing—stuff I could do in my sleep. I know the systems inside and out, I took a few supply chain classes back in the day that help with the inventory software, I've got decades of experience on the dock... I am completely, one hundred percent job-ready. I keep telling myself that, and I keep telling them that. I'm ready to go right this second. 

But... the company requires this standard medical clearance before they can unfreeze my start date and actually put me on the payroll. And that clinic doctor—the one I mentioned earlier who completely panicked over the scale—he absolutely refuses to sign the paperwork. He flagged my file. So now, the new logistics job won’t clear me to start until I get this so-called issue addressed. Because of his hang-ups about my eating habits and my weight, my entire work plan is completely on hold. 

It's driving me up the wall, doc. I wake up at four-thirty, I do my walk, I have my black coffee, and then... nothing. I don't have a dock to go to. I'm just sitting on my hands, pacing around the house, while some doctor who doesn't know the first thing about freight lines decides if I'm allowed to earn a living.
